items.question: What is the primary purpose of an audit trail in a Claude-integrated workflow?

options.A: To prevent Claude from producing outputs that violate organisational policy.
options.B: To create a record of what Claude produced, who reviewed it, and what actions were taken, enabling accountability and reconstruction.
options.C: To block the workflow when Claude's outputs fall below a quality threshold.
options.D: To cache prompt-response pairs so identical requests return consistent results.

items.question: What is an escalation path in a Claude-integrated workflow?

options.A: A process for switching to a more capable model tier when Claude's output quality is insufficient.
options.B: A pre-defined route that directs cases exceeding Claude's handling capability to a human or an alternative process.
options.C: A logging mechanism that records when Claude's outputs are flagged for quality review.
options.D: A prompt engineering strategy for gradually increasing task complexity across turns.

items.question: Which TWO of the following accurately describe a connector in Claude workflow integration? (Choose TWO)

options.A: A connector is a one-time file upload that must be repeated each session to remain current.
options.B: A connector provides Claude with live or regularly refreshed access to an external system or data source.
options.C: A connector requires no API or system integration; it operates entirely within the chat interface.
options.D: A connector enables data to flow in both directions — from external systems into Claude and from Claude's outputs back to those systems.
options.E: A connector is only available to users on the Claude API and cannot be used through claude.ai.

items.question: What does 'designing for auditability' require in a Claude-integrated workflow?

options.A: Using the highest-tier model to ensure the most accurate output is always recorded.
options.B: Building the workflow so that every material decision and its inputs, reviewers, and outcomes can be reconstructed after the fact.
options.C: Requiring human approval for every Claude output regardless of content or risk level.
options.D: Storing Claude's raw API responses in a database before any human sees them.

items.question: Which TWO of the following are essential properties of a well-designed handoff from a Claude step to a system of record? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Claude's output is written to the system of record in its raw form without any transformation.
options.B: The handoff includes validation that Claude's output meets the system of record's format and acceptance criteria before writing.
options.C: The handoff is triggered as soon as Claude returns a response, with no intermediate step.
options.D: The record written captures not only Claude's output but also sufficient context to reconstruct why that output was written.
options.E: The system of record is updated in real time regardless of whether a human review step has been completed.

items.question: What is the most precise distinction between a human-in-the-loop checkpoint and an approval gate?

options.A: Human-in-the-loop means a human reviews output; an approval gate means the review is automated.
options.B: Human-in-the-loop is a broader pattern covering any human review role; an approval gate is a specific instance that blocks the workflow until explicit sign-off is granted.
options.C: Human-in-the-loop applies only to Claude outputs; an approval gate applies to any stage in a business process.
options.D: Human-in-the-loop is used in interactive workflows; approval gates are used in batch workflows.

items.question: What does an audit trail provide that a human-in-the-loop checkpoint does NOT?

options.A: A mechanism to prevent incorrect outputs from reaching downstream systems.
options.B: A retrospective record that allows decisions and their context to be reconstructed after the workflow has run.
options.C: A designated human reviewer who acts on Claude's output before it is used.
options.D: A quality filter that blocks outputs below a defined standard.

items.question: When is an approval gate required rather than a softer review checkpoint?

options.A: When the workflow processes more than one hundred items per day.
options.B: When the downstream action is irreversible or carries consequences that the organisation cannot accept if based on an unreviewed error.
options.C: When Claude's model tier is Haiku and a higher-confidence output is needed.
options.D: When the workflow has been running for fewer than thirty days and the error rate has not been established.

items.question: What is the most significant operational difference between a connector and a per-session file upload as a data source for Claude?

options.A: A connector can handle larger files than a per-session upload.
options.B: A connector maintains a persistent link that keeps the data Claude accesses current; an upload is a static snapshot that becomes stale over time.
options.C: A connector is restricted to structured data; per-session uploads support unstructured text.
options.D: A per-session upload persists across multiple users in a shared Project; a connector is private to a single session.

items.question: What property of a workflow step makes straight-through processing inappropriate regardless of Claude's accuracy on that step?

options.A: The step processes more than fifty items per hour.
options.B: The step's output requires formatting before it can be read by the next system.
options.C: The step's downstream action is irreversible and cannot be corrected before causing material harm.
options.D: The step involves text that includes personal data subject to privacy policy.

items.question: Which TWO statements correctly distinguish a fallback path from an escalation path in workflow design? (Choose TWO)

options.A: A fallback path responds to a Claude failure or refusal; an escalation path responds to a case that exceeds the workflow's defined scope.
options.B: Fallback and escalation are synonyms; both describe routing cases to human handlers.
options.C: A fallback path may include non-human responses such as retrying a modified prompt or returning a safe default; an escalation path always routes to a human.
options.D: Both fallback and escalation paths should be defined during workflow design, not added reactively after failures occur.
options.E: An escalation path is only needed in high-volume batch workflows; fallback paths apply to all workflow types.

items.question: What is the PRIMARY risk of removing all human review from a Claude workflow step that writes to a system of record?

options.A: The workflow becomes dependent on a single model tier that may be deprecated.
options.B: Claude's outputs may contain errors that become permanently embedded in business data before they can be detected and corrected.
options.C: The absence of human review prevents the workflow from being scaled to higher volumes.
options.D: Claude's token usage increases when no human feedback is provided between steps.

items.question: What is the primary benefit of using a prompt template for a team-wide Claude workflow?

options.A: It locks in the model tier so that all team members use the same level of reasoning capability.
options.B: It ensures consistent output quality across team members by standardising the instructions Claude receives.
options.C: It prevents team members from modifying prompts in ways that could improve results.
options.D: It reduces Claude's token usage by compressing repeated instructions automatically.

items.question: What distinguishes a pilot from a full rollout in AI workflow deployment?

options.A: A pilot uses a lower model tier to reduce cost; a full rollout upgrades to the production tier.
options.B: A pilot is a limited-scope deployment used to test and learn before committing to organisation-wide adoption.
options.C: A pilot is run by the vendor; a full rollout is managed by the organisation's own team.
options.D: A pilot processes synthetic data only; a full rollout processes real business data.

items.question: Why must a baseline be established before measuring the success of a Claude workflow integration?

options.A: To set the model tier configuration before the first prompt is run.
options.B: Without a baseline, there is no reference point against which to measure whether the integration improved performance.
options.C: To comply with data retention requirements that mandate performance records prior to AI use.
options.D: To prevent team members from using the workflow before it has been formally approved.

items.question: What does 'standardising Claude usage across a team' primarily achieve?

options.A: It eliminates the need for individual team members to understand prompt engineering.
options.B: It ensures that similar tasks produce comparable results regardless of which team member runs them.
options.C: It restricts Claude usage to a single approved use case, preventing workflow scope creep.
options.D: It automatically logs all team member interactions with Claude for compliance purposes.

items.question: Which design principle should govern the scope of a Claude workflow pilot?

options.A: The pilot should include all intended users to generate statistically meaningful quality data.
options.B: The pilot should be small enough to be reversible and bounded but realistic enough to generate meaningful learning.
options.C: The pilot should run for no more than two weeks to minimise the cost of delay if the workflow is unsuitable.
options.D: The pilot should use historical data only so that errors have no real operational impact.

items.question: What must workflow documentation include for other team members to run a Claude-integrated process independently?

options.A: A full transcript of the workflow developer's conversation with Claude during the design phase.
options.B: The step-by-step process, prompt templates, review criteria, escalation triggers, and any known edge-case handling.
options.C: The model tier configuration file and API key used by the workflow developer.
options.D: A list of team members authorised to run the workflow and their training completion dates.

items.question: Which TWO of the following are characteristics of effective success metrics for a Claude workflow integration? (Choose TWO)

options.A: They are defined after the pilot so that actual results inform what constitutes success.
options.B: They are tied to business outcomes rather than to Claude's technical performance alone.
options.C: They compare post-integration performance against a pre-defined baseline.
options.D: They measure exclusively how often Claude's outputs require correction by a human reviewer.
options.E: They are established by the model vendor rather than by the organisation using the workflow.

items.question: What is the role of change management in a Claude workflow rollout?

options.A: To update Claude's system prompt when the workflow's requirements change over time.
options.B: To help users understand, adopt, and effectively use the new AI-assisted workflow, addressing concerns and building confidence.
options.C: To migrate all existing documents into Claude Projects before the rollout begins.
options.D: To enforce compliance with the new workflow by tracking and reporting non-adoption to leadership.

items.question: Which TWO of the following most commonly explain why AI adoption remains uneven across a team after a workflow has been deployed? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Some team members have not been given access to Claude.
options.B: Individual team members have different levels of confidence in AI-generated output and different willingness to change habitual workflows.
options.C: The workflow produces different quality outputs for different users because of variations in individual prompt usage.
options.D: Claude performs differently depending on the user's seniority or role title.
options.E: The organisation has not defined which tasks the workflow applies to.

items.question: When should a Claude workflow be sunset rather than iteratively improved?

options.A: When a newer version of Claude's model tier becomes available and migration is required.
options.B: When the underlying business process the workflow serves is itself being discontinued or replaced.
options.C: When more than twenty percent of the workflow's outputs require human correction.
options.D: When the team that originally designed the workflow has been reassigned.

items.question: What is the defining operational difference between a pilot and a full rollout of a Claude workflow?

options.A: A pilot uses sandbox data; a full rollout uses production data.
options.B: A pilot is bounded and reversible with defined learning goals; a full rollout commits the organisation to ongoing operational use.
options.C: A pilot is managed by the IT department; a full rollout is managed by the business unit.
options.D: A pilot runs Claude outputs past an additional approval layer that the full rollout omits.

items.question: What distinguishes ROI from success metrics in the evaluation of a Claude workflow integration?

options.A: ROI is a lagging financial calculation comparing costs to measurable business gains; success metrics include a broader set of leading and lagging indicators of workflow performance.
options.B: ROI is measured by the IT team; success metrics are measured by the business unit.
options.C: ROI only applies to cost-reduction workflows; success metrics apply to quality-improvement workflows.
options.D: Success metrics are defined after the workflow launches; ROI is estimated before launch.

items.question: In workflow evaluation, what distinguishes a leading indicator from a lagging indicator?

options.A: Leading indicators are measured by humans; lagging indicators are measured automatically.
options.B: A leading indicator signals likely future performance early enough to intervene; a lagging indicator confirms what has already occurred.
options.C: Leading indicators measure the workflow's technical performance; lagging indicators measure user satisfaction.
options.D: Lagging indicators are more reliable than leading indicators and should be prioritised in measurement frameworks.

items.question: What is the key difference between standardising Claude usage through prompt templates and standardising it through training?

options.A: Templates enforce standardisation at execution time; training builds capability that allows users to adapt intelligently when the template does not fit.
options.B: Templates are more expensive to maintain than training programmes.
options.C: Training is required before templates can be used; templates are not usable without prior training.
options.D: Templates apply to batch workflows; training is required for interactive workflows.

items.question: Which TWO actions are most critical when scaling a Claude workflow from one power user to an entire department? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Encoding the power user's best prompt practices into shared templates accessible to all team members.
options.B: Assigning the power user as the permanent sole operator of the workflow to maintain quality.
options.C: Documenting the workflow steps, review criteria, and known edge cases so others can run it independently.
options.D: Upgrading to a higher model tier to compensate for less-experienced users.
options.E: Transferring ownership of the workflow from the power user to the IT department.

items.question: Which condition most clearly justifies sunsetting a Claude workflow rather than continuing to iterate on it?

options.A: The workflow's outputs require more human correction than originally projected.
options.B: Iteration has produced no improvement over multiple cycles and the root cause is a fundamental task-fit mismatch rather than a prompt design problem.
options.C: The team that built the workflow has been reorganised and no one has ownership of the template.
options.D: A competing workflow built by a different team produces higher quality outputs on the same task.

items.question: What is 'straight-through processing' in a Claude-integrated workflow?

options.A: Running a prompt without any system-level instructions to keep the interaction direct.
options.B: Processing all inputs in a batch rather than one at a time.
options.C: Forwarding Claude's output directly to a downstream system or action without any human review step.
options.D: Using a single prompt to handle multiple task types in sequence.

items.question: What is a connector in the context of Claude workflow integration?

options.A: A prompt template that links multiple task steps in a single conversation turn.
options.B: An integration that gives Claude persistent, live access to an external data source or system.
options.C: A Claude Project that connects multiple team members to a shared knowledge base.
options.D: A formatted output that can be imported directly into another software application.

items.question: What distinguishes a pilot from a proof of concept in AI workflow deployment?

options.A: A proof of concept tests technical feasibility with simplified or synthetic data; a pilot tests real-world performance with genuine business inputs.
options.B: A proof of concept involves the entire user population; a pilot involves only the technical team.
options.C: A proof of concept is conducted after the pilot to validate that findings can be replicated at scale.
options.D: A pilot tests a single prompt; a proof of concept tests the full workflow.

items.question: In workflow design, which assessment must come before the other: task suitability or task decomposition?

options.A: Task decomposition, because you cannot assess suitability without first understanding the workflow's individual steps.
options.B: Task suitability, because decomposition is only worth undertaking for processes that have already been assessed as candidates for AI involvement.
options.C: They are conducted simultaneously to avoid bias in either direction.
options.D: Task decomposition comes first for batch workflows; task suitability comes first for interactive workflows.

items.question: Which latency characteristic is the defining signal that a workflow is suited for batch rather than interactive Claude integration?

options.A: The workflow requires responses in under two seconds per item.
options.B: The workflow benefits from discussion and iterative refinement during processing.
options.C: A delay between input submission and output receipt is acceptable within the workflow's operating requirements.
options.D: The workflow's outputs are time-stamped to comply with regulatory reporting deadlines.

items.question: Which property is present in an approval gate but NOT necessarily in all human-in-the-loop checkpoints?

options.A: The involvement of a human reviewer at some point in the workflow.
options.B: The creation of a record that the review occurred.
options.C: An explicit blocking mechanism that prevents the workflow from proceeding until sign-off is received.
options.D: The ability to modify Claude's output before the workflow continues.

items.question: Which property is present in a connector but absent in a per-session file upload used as a Claude data source?

options.A: The ability to provide Claude with text-formatted input.
options.B: Persistence across sessions and automatic refresh as the source data changes.
options.C: Support for documents larger than can be typed into a chat message.
options.D: The option to restrict which team members can access the provided data.

items.question: Which TWO questions must a pilot answer before a Claude workflow can be responsibly approved for full rollout? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Does the workflow produce outputs of acceptable quality on real business inputs?
options.B: Has the model vendor confirmed that the tier used will not be deprecated?
options.C: Do target users adopt and effectively use the workflow in practice?
options.D: Has the workflow been reviewed by an external AI auditor?
options.E: Is the cost per API call within the organisation's pre-defined technical budget?

items.question: What is the key timing difference between an audit trail and an approval gate in a Claude workflow?

options.A: An audit trail is set up before the workflow runs; an approval gate is configured after the first failure.
options.B: An audit trail operates retrospectively, recording events after they occur; an approval gate operates prospectively, blocking the flow before an event proceeds.
options.C: An approval gate records decisions before they happen; an audit trail reviews them afterward.
options.D: Both operate prospectively but at different points in the workflow sequence.

items.question: Which TWO actions distinguish rolling out a Claude workflow to a department from simply scaling it to more users? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Rollout includes change management, training, and communication to help users understand and adopt the workflow.
options.B: Scaling requires switching to a more powerful model tier to handle the increased volume.
options.C: Rollout establishes governance structures: ownership, version control for templates, and a feedback channel for issues.
options.D: Scaling only involves providing more users with access credentials; no other changes are needed.
options.E: Rollout is managed by the vendor; scaling is managed by the organisation.

items.question: A workflow has an audit trail but no human-in-the-loop checkpoint. Which risk does this create that adding a HITL checkpoint would address?

options.A: The audit trail's records may be incomplete because there is no reviewer to confirm what Claude produced.
options.B: Claude's outputs are forwarded to downstream systems before any human has the opportunity to catch and correct errors.
options.C: The workflow cannot demonstrate compliance because audit trails are not accepted as compliance evidence without a co-located HITL checkpoint.
options.D: The absence of HITL means the audit trail itself will not be generated.

items.question: A workflow relies on Claude querying a policy document that is updated monthly. Which data source design correctly addresses the currency requirement?

options.A: Upload the document at the start of each session and rely on session persistence to maintain access throughout the day.
options.B: Store the document in a Claude Project knowledge base and update it manually each month after the new version is published.
options.C: Use a connector to the document management system so Claude always accesses the current version without manual intervention.
options.D: Include the key policy clauses directly in the system prompt, updating the system prompt each month.

items.question: Why is reversibility a defining property of a pilot and not of a full rollout?

options.A: A pilot uses synthetic data that can be discarded; a full rollout embeds data in systems of record.
options.B: A pilot is intentionally bounded so that stopping it causes minimal operational disruption; a full rollout integrates the workflow into normal operations, making it much harder to withdraw.
options.C: A pilot requires regulatory approval to begin; a full rollout does not.
options.D: A pilot is reversible because it runs on a separate technical infrastructure that can be decommissioned independently.

items.question: Which scenario correctly identifies the factor that makes batch, not interactive, the appropriate integration choice?

options.A: A team wants to produce higher quality outputs by using Opus instead of Sonnet; Opus is only available in batch mode.
options.B: A nightly processing job collects the day's incoming documents and processes all of them before the next business morning; immediate per-document results are not required.
options.C: A workflow involves sensitive data that must not be visible in a chat interface at any point during processing.
options.D: The team's IT policy prohibits real-time API calls and mandates scheduled processing for all automated workflows.

items.question: Which TWO properties are unique to a connector as a Claude data source, compared to a per-session file upload? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The connector allows Claude to access data that was not uploaded by the user in the current session.
options.B: The connector can be used across multiple Claude sessions without re-establishing the data source each time.
options.C: The connector provides Claude with access to images and non-text content.
options.D: The connector requires a prompt template to function correctly.
options.E: The connector supports a larger total context window than a file upload.

items.question: What does an approval gate add to a workflow that a non-blocking review checkpoint does not?

options.A: A designated human reviewer who examines Claude's output.
options.B: A record of who reviewed the output and when.
options.C: A hard stop that prevents any downstream action from proceeding without explicit authorisation.
options.D: The ability to modify Claude's output before it reaches the downstream system.

items.question: Which event is the clearest signal that a Claude workflow should be sunset rather than maintained?

options.A: The workflow's prompt templates have not been updated in six months.
options.B: The business process the workflow supports has been discontinued.
options.C: Claude's output correction rate has risen above the team's acceptable threshold.
options.D: Fewer than half the eligible team members use the workflow regularly.

items.question: What does 'enablement' mean in the context of team Claude adoption?

options.A: Granting API access permissions to all team members simultaneously.
options.B: Building the knowledge, skills, and confidence that allow team members to use Claude-assisted workflows effectively and independently.
options.C: Publishing prompt templates in a shared location accessible to the team.
options.D: Configuring Claude to automatically adapt its output format to each individual user's preferences.

items.question: Which of the following is most important to capture in a baseline before deploying a Claude workflow for task automation?

options.A: The number of team members who have prior experience using AI tools.
options.B: The current time, error rate, and volume per period for the tasks being automated.
options.C: The API pricing tier the organisation plans to use for the integration.
options.D: The model tier currently used by competitor organisations for similar tasks.

items.question: Why does removing all human review from a high-volume Claude workflow create compounding risk over time?

options.A: Claude's error rate increases as the volume of items processed rises.
options.B: Each error propagates to a downstream system without detection, and the absolute number of errors grows proportionally with volume, potentially embedding many errors before any are caught.
options.C: High-volume workflows exhaust the model's context window, reducing output quality for later items in the batch.
options.D: Removing human review prevents the organisation from tracking which items were processed, creating an audit gap.

items.question: How does using a shared prompt template reduce output variability across a team?

options.A: It forces Claude to produce identical outputs for all inputs, regardless of input differences.
options.B: It ensures all team members provide Claude with the same instructions, constraints, and format expectations, so quality differences come only from genuine input variation rather than from differences in how individuals phrase prompts.
options.C: It restricts Claude's vocabulary so outputs match a predefined word list.
options.D: It caches outputs from previous runs so Claude does not re-generate responses for common inputs.

items.question: Which element of change management most directly prevents resistant users from undermining a Claude workflow rollout?

options.A: Monitoring which team members are using the workflow and reporting low adopters to their managers.
options.B: Involving representative users in the design and piloting phases so they have input into the workflow and familiarity with it before rollout.
options.C: Making the old manual process technically unavailable so users must use the workflow.
options.D: Publishing the business case for the workflow so users understand the financial rationale.
